### Genealogical and Epistemological Dimensions

The foundational concepts of parasocial relationships were first established by sociologists Donald Horton and R. Richard Wohl (1956) when they observed a unique phenomenon born from the infancy of radio and television mass media. During this era, home viewers developed a sense of intimacy, attachment, and pseudo-closeness toward public figures appearing before them—a news anchor, a soap opera actor, or a talk show host. Horton and Wohl recognized that this interaction possessed a fundamental epistemological flaw: it was strictly one-sided. The figure on the screen never knew, remembered, or personally reciprocated the viewer's feelings. This relationship was sustained through the illusion of face-to-face engagement, wherein the human subject projected affective needs, social validation, and companionship into a media vacuum, while the media object remained cold, programmed, and indifferent behind electromagnetic waves (Weizenbaum, 1976).

However, the third decade of the twenty-first century has shattered the structural asymmetry that historically characterized traditional parasocial relationships. With the advent of Large Language Models and transformer-based conversational agents, this one-way relationship has mutated into what we may define as an *interactive parasocial relationship*. This is no longer merely gazing at a silent wax mask behind a glass screen; it is a rhetorical mirror that actively responds, reshapes its own structure, and reflects back every fragment of psychological vulnerability fed into it by the user. From an epistemological standpoint, a radical shift has occurred from *observing* to *interacting* (Floridi, 2013). Algorithms no longer merely broadcast static narratives; instead, they weave dynamic, adaptive, and highly personalized narrative webs that exploit human evolutionary instincts, which are biologically hardwired to detect consciousness, intent, and empathy in other entities (Searle, 1980; Turing, 1950).

The genealogy of this disruption brings us to the realization that humans are phylogenetically predisposed to be easily deceived by social cues (Dreyfus, 1972). As Nass and Reeves (1996) famously demonstrated in their classic experiments through "The Media Equation" paradigm, the human brain reacts to computer media in the exact same manner as it does when interacting with fellow human beings. We feel polite toward computers, we feel intimidated by interface reprimands, and we instinctively place trust in a friendly synthetic voice. While legacy broadcast technology merely triggered surface-level empathy circuits, generative artificial intelligence stimulates deep attachment circuitry—regions of the brain typically reserved for caregiver-infant bonds, intimate friendships, or romantic eros (Bowlby, 1969). Consequently, classical parasocial theory, once deployed to explain soap opera addiction, must now be rewritten as a framework for understanding how binary code can hijack the human affective architecture (Zuboff, 2019).

This epistemological transformation also fundamentally alters how we define "presence" within digital spaces. In the broadcasting era, presence was a spatial illusion; in the era of generative AI, presence is a *reciprocal illusion*. Users do not feel as though they are operating software tools; rather, they feel accompanied by an entity possessing infinite attention—a digital manifestation of Martin Buber's (1923) dialogical principle, wherein the "I" treats the algorithm not as an object (*Es*), but as a pseudo-subject (*Du*). When a language model responds to a lonely individual's confession at three in the morning with phrases that are warm, lexically empathetic, and contextually consistent, the user's cognitive architecture instantly overrides the material fact that the entity is merely a collection of multidimensional matrix probability weights. Herein lies the ultimate irony of modernity: we have created hyper-rational technology rooted in pure mathematics, yet the primary instrument it deploys to conquer the market is its ability to trigger our most primordial emotional irrationalities (Kahneman, 2011).
